title: ⭐ Practice: the words of the school day

questions.prompt: Four words from the school day, and the four that answer them. Match each one with its opposite.
questions.explanation: Four pairs, and each of them turns on a different kind of contrast. Two are the two ends of a single act, seen from the two sides of the desk: one person passes the knowledge on and the other takes it in; one person sits the paper while the other sets it and marks it. The third is a matter of staying or going, since a name stands on the register for years and then one day it is taken off. And the fourth cuts the calendar in two, because every week of a school year falls on one side of it or on the other. Take them by meaning: two of these pairs are verbs and two are nouns, so the shape of a word narrows the field but never finishes the job for you.

questions.prompt: Sami takes a report home in December, in March and in June, and that is his whole year in Sfax. His cousin in Boston takes one home in January and one in May, and that is her whole year. What is one of those pieces of the year called in each of the two systems?

options.text: a term in the first system, a chapter in the second
a semester in the first system, a term in the second
a timetable in the first system, a term in the second
a term in the first system, a semester in the second

questions.explanation: Count the reports and you have counted the pieces: three of them in Sfax, two in Boston. Three pieces and each one is a term; two pieces and each one is a semester — a word that admits what it is, since it opens on the same syllable as semicircle and semifinal, and half a year is exactly what it covers. The other two answers borrow words that name something else: one names the grid of the week, the other one of the divisions of a book.

questions.prompt: A teacher says out loud, writing nothing on the board: "Take four away from twenty, then share what is left equally among the four pupils in the front row." Which two operations has she asked for, in that order?
questions.explanation: Ordinary speech hides the four operations behind everyday phrases, and two of them are here: take away asks for the minus sign, and share equally among asks for the division sign. Nothing in the sentence asks for a product — that would have been said with times or with lots of. And the order is not a detail: taking four from twenty and then sharing between four leaves each pupil with four, whereas sharing first and taking four away afterwards leaves one. Same two verbs, same two numbers, two different answers.

questions.prompt: A librarian pins a notice under the top shelf: "These books are too high up for the youngest readers to reach on their own." Who is unable to do what?

options.text: the librarian cannot reach the books
the youngest readers cannot reach the books
the youngest readers cannot be reached
the books cannot reach the youngest readers

questions.explanation: When this structure carries a for, the noun standing behind that little word hands the second verb its doer: here it is the small children, and reaching is what they cannot do. The librarian is nowhere in the sentence, and the shelf being high up is a fact about her stock, not about her arms. Nor is anything passive here: the readers do the reaching, they do not undergo it. And a shelf full of books has never reached for anybody.

questions.prompt: You are writing an acrostic on the word SCHOOL. Each line has to begin with the letter that falls to it, and each line has to open with a verb saying what a school does for you. You have reached the fourth letter, O. Which of these words may stand at the head of that line?
questions.explanation: All four begin with the right letter, which is precisely why the letter decides nothing. The model asks for a verb, an action the place performs on you, and only one of these four can be conjugated: a school offers you a library, a trade, a second chance. The three others belong to other classes — one tells you how often something happens, one describes a thing and is the very word hiding behind the O of O level, and one names something you hold rather than something you do.

questions.prompt: A pupil writes in his English diary: "Yesterday I assisted at the science lesson." He means only that he was there, sitting with his class and taking notes. What should he have written?

options.text: Yesterday I attended the science lesson.
Yesterday I assisted the science lesson.
Yesterday I attended at the science lesson.
Yesterday I presented the science lesson.

questions.explanation: Being present at a lesson is said with one verb, and that verb reaches its object directly, without any small word in between. Two traps are set around it. The first is a verb that looks the same in French but has crossed the Channel with another job: in English it means to help, so keeping it would claim that the pupil lent the teacher a hand. The second is subtler, because it repairs the verb and keeps the preposition, which English simply does not want there. And promoting him to the one who presents the lesson would make him the person giving it, not the person sitting through it.
